title: Pauri 11: listening, the blind find the way
hookLine: suniai: by listening the blind find the path and the unfathomable becomes clear (Japji 11)

cards: The power goes out at night. The screen dies, the room goes black, and for a second you're lost in your own home. Then you start listening.
The fridge is silent, so the kitchen is there. The clock ticks on the left. A car passes, so the window is ahead.
Without planning to, you've made a map out of sound, and you find the door. Someone who lives without sight may do this with far more skill, reading a street by its echoes.
After three stanzas of suniai, by listening, Japji reaches for that picture: finding your way in the dark.

teach.b: Pauri 11 is the fourth and last of the suniai stanzas, a string of short lines each starting with the same word. Its central line, in Guru Nanak's own words: suniai andhe paavahi raahu.

By listening, the blind find the road. Around it, in paraphrase: by listening, a person dives deep into oceans of virtue. By listening, ordinary people become like the shaikhs, the pirs and the kings.
And by listening, what was fathomless comes within your hand. The word there is asagaah, water too deep to wade across. Listening doesn't drain the ocean.
It puts the far shore in reach. So who are the blind?

Sikh commentators read this as a blindness anyone can have: not knowing which way to go, stumbling around in our own ego. It isn't a promise about eyes, and it isn't a remark about people who can't see.
It's the power cut again: when you can't see the way, you can still hear it. Hear what? In Japji, the Name and the Guru's word, the shabad.
The listening is what turns into direction.
Then the stanza closes like the other three, for the last time in a while: Nanak says the devotees are always in bloom, and by listening, pain and wrongdoing are wiped away. Four stanzas, one lesson.
Before you can trust, before you can walk, you listen.

how: Many Sikhs recite Japji Sahib every morning as part of Nitnem; Pauri 11 is the last of the four stanzas that begin suniai, by listening, and each of those four ends with the same refrain.

o: blind, unable to see the road ahead
fathomless, water too deep to wade across
a shallow stream you can step across

games.q: what's inside Pauri 11 — tap the pairs.
p: the devotees are always in bloom

s: Pauri 11 promises that listening will heal eyesight
commentators read the blindness as not knowing the way, which anyone can share.
Pauri 11 is the last of four stanzas that begin suniai
pauris 8 to 11 all begin by listening, and all end with the same refrain.
in Japji, the listening is to the Name and the Guru's word
the shabad is what the listener hears, and it becomes direction.

games.q: you're standing at the edge of water too deep to wade. what does Pauri 11 say puts the far side in reach?
games.why: by listening, what was fathomless comes within your hand. the water stays deep; the shore comes in reach.

practice: Close your eyes and let the sounds arrive, without naming them at first. Then let them slowly make a map: what's near, what's far, what's to your left, what's behind you, how much of the room you can find without looking.
If a thought pulls you away, come back by finding where one sound is coming from.

wordCard.voice: Asagaah. Fathomless, water too deep to wade across: by listening, it comes within reach, and the blind find the road.

orig.note: Gurmukhi, Japji Pauri 11: by listening, the blind find the road.

carryVoice: Your line: the blind find the way. When looking fails, listening can still point. That's day one hundred eighty-one.
